items.title: China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?
items.summary: The talks are expected to focus on issues including nuclear non-proliferation, the Middle East war, trade policies and, possibly, the Ukraine war.
items.content:
China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin meeting in first three-way summit
The talks are expected to focus on issues including nuclear non-proliferation, the Middle East war, trade policies and, possibly, the Ukraine war.
The three-way summit among the three nations is unprecedented.
"The ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first-among-equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit" for Beijing: analyst.
Russian artist Alexey Sergienko unveils his new pop art painting dubbed "Shenzhen, 26" in Saint Petersburg on November 12, 2026.
China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.
That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.
While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.
"For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.
Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.
The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda.
"He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world , whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call . The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.
Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.
China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.
China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement.
"Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability."
A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.
Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.
U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

items.title: Canada bars Russia from Junior World Championships
items.summary: Canada says it will not allow Russian athletes to compete in the Junior Ice Hockey World Championships because of the war in Ukraine.
items.content:
Image caption, Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022
Russia's hopes of reintegration into international sport suffered a setback when it was barred from the upcoming Junior Ice Hockey World Championships.
Canada said it would deny entry to Russian athletes as a result of the war in Ukraine.
"Due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian government, the Russian Under-20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship," the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement.
It said that "after carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer."
The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable and unlawful" and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
"The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons," it said in a statement.
"The exclusion of the Russian national team violates fundamental legal principles, Olympism, the principle of non-discrimination, equality among athletes and the integrity of international tournaments."
Russia had been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, but last month the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned the ban.
It said that the IIHF's arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence" and ordered it to allow Russia to participate in its events.
The move was welcomed by Russia but condemned by Ukraine and along with some sponsors of the Junior World Championships.
Six European ice hockey federations said they would refuse to play Russia if they were allowed to take part, appearing to leave the tournament in limbo.
On Wednesday the Canadian government said it would deny visas to any Russian athletes, effectively barring them from participating.
It is the latest example of a wider backlash against efforts to allow Russia to return to international sport.
This week Norway, Finland and Estonia said they would block visas for Russian and Belarusian athletes.
Norway is preparing to host skiing's Cross-country World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the Figure Skating World Championships in March.
The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.
In March several athletes from Russia and Belarus were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.
In July the IOC provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, saying a ban introduced in 2023 was "no longer applicable".
However, sports federations can enforce their own eligibility criteria.
While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.
Last month it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the invasion of Ukraine.

items.content:
Ret Brig Gen warns Iran's military capabilities are not at zero
Ret. Brig. Gen. John Teichert discusses Iran’s military capabilities following a drone attack aimed at Bahrain on ‘America Reports.’
Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned Saturday that airstrikes alone may not eliminate Iran's weapons capabilities, but said a U.S. ground invasion would be an "absolute disaster."
Speaking at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi, Blinken, who served under President Biden, pointed to Iran's massive territory, population of roughly 90 million and ability to produce weapons deep inside the country as obstacles to any military campaign aimed at dismantling its arsenal.
"The weapons that it continues to produce are back far enough, the range is great enough that you can't just take everything out," Blinken said. "You'd probably have to have a land invasion of some kind to do that, which would be an absolute disaster."
TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING
Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken said President Donald Trump's 20-point ceasefire agreement was based on the one developed by the Biden administration. (ARMEND NIMANI/AFP via Getty Images)
Blinken's warning came ahead of Iran claiming Sunday to have launched six drones at a U.S. military installation in Bahrain, while reports surfaced that neighboring Iraq faced concerns that its territory could be drawn into a potential American ground operation.
Bahrain said its air defenses blocked several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, the first such interceptions since September.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted a U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base with six drones in retaliation for what it described as "hostile US actions," according to Iranian state media, Reuters reported.
Bahraini officials said the drones were intercepted before reaching their targets.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
The locations of U.S. bases throughout the Gulf are seen in relation to Iran. (Fox News)
The latest escalation came amid further fighting in Yemen, where the Houthis made advances against Saudi-backed forces , raising additional concerns about the conflict spreading across the region.
Blinken warned that Iran retains the ability to widen the confrontation despite the United States' overwhelming conventional military superiority.
While Washington can "escalate vertically" by intensifying its bombing campaign, Blinken said, Tehran can "escalate horizontally" by targeting American military installations, regional allies and critical infrastructure, either directly or through allied armed groups.
"Even though we're much more powerful, that asymmetry in their ability to escalate horizontally as opposed to vertically is not to our advantage," Blinken said.
The former top diplomat also emphasized the geographic challenges facing U.S. forces.
"That coastline along the Strait of Hormuz goes on forever," Blinken said.
Iran is roughly four times the size of California, with a coastline and weapons production facilities that could complicate efforts to eliminate its military capabilities through air power alone.
TRUMP'S MOAB THREAT COULD PUT IRAN'S DEEPEST BUNKERS IN AMERICA'S CROSSHAIRS
Soldiers from the US-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the US-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq on March 29, 2020. (Soldiers from the US-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the US-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq on March 29, 2020)
Concerns about a potential ground operation have also intensified in neighboring Iraq, where officials have resisted proposals to sharply restrict trade and movement across the Iranian border.
Iran International reported that Tehran has become concerned that Iraqi territory could be used as a staging ground for a potential U.S. operation into southern Iran.
The Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada reported Nov. 9 that Iraq's prime minister privately briefed Shiite political leaders on an alleged American military plan involving a ground offensive, the outlet said.
In an interview with France 24 published Friday, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein had also warned that the region's unstable security environment could not continue indefinitely.
The current state of "no war and no peace" is unsustainable, Hussein said, warning that the confrontation "either goes towards peace or it goes towards war."
AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?
An MH-60R Sea Hawk helicopter lands on the flight deck of USS Rafael Peralta as it transits regional waters, in this photo released by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 15, 2026. CENTCOM said the USS Rafael Peralta is enforcing a military blockade of Iranian ports. (CENTCOM)
Hussein also said Baghdad has a responsibility to pursue diplomatic mediation because Iraq has already been drawn into the conflict.
He pointed to recent outreach to Tehran, including discussions with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.
The Iraqi foreign minister also rejected a reported U.S. demand that Baghdad close all but two of its land border crossings with Iran, describing the proposed restrictions as "not possible" and "a kind of sanction against the Iraqi people."
The border dispute comes as U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) expands efforts to disrupt Iranian weapons shipments and illicit trade through Task Force Iron Gate .
CENTCOM announced the task force would coordinate with other U.S. agencies to prevent Iran from transporting advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue across its land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

items.title: Trump’s Hormuz squeeze has Iran strangled — now slam its back door, too - New York Post
items.summary: Trump’s Hormuz squeeze has Iran strangled — now slam its back door, too  New York Post
items.content:
Cargo trucks halted at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing at the border between Pakistan and Iran during a temporary suspension of trade on Oct. 21, 2026.
America no longer needs a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump proclaimed last week.
“We’ve got their money . . . and we’ve got their Strait!” he wrote Thursday.
He’s right about the Strait of Hormuz: Gulf oil is flowing through the passage again under US Navy escort, despite Iranian attacks on shipping — but Iran hasn’t loaded a barrel of oil onto a ship since Aug. 25.
Before the US blockade, Iran’s southern sea routes carried as much as 80% of its trade.
What still reaches Tehran comes mostly by land, across seven international borders .
Those roads have become the regime’s lifeline. It’s now time to close them.
American blockades at sea and in the air demonstrate what effective enforcement can do.
In March, the first month of the war, almost no crude oil from the Arab countries passed through Hormuz; in October, 10.3 million barrels a day did, about three-quarters of the prewar flow.
But the US Navy has bottled up Iran’s tanker fleet, and that’s inflicted real damage: In mid-October Iran sold the last of the 89 million barrels it had on tankers beyond the blockade line.
Its Chinese buyers pay a month or two after delivery, so the final payments could arrive around mid-December.
Now, a senior budget official is saying Tehran “must prepare for circumstances in which oil revenue reaches zero.”
The sky is closing too : Since Treasury sanctioned the last of Iran’s airlines in September, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan have barred them all.
China’s and Russia’s are the last major runways still open.
The roads, however, are allowing the regime to rearm and to buy time.
At least $2 billion in military supplies has reached Iran since January 2025, some of it by truck from Central Asia.
A land blockade doesn’t mean sealing 3,700 miles of frontier.
Heavy freight must pass through a limited number of official crossings, and trucks cannot carry the loads that ships do: An official at Iran’s own Chamber of Commerce has estimated that one cargo vessel equals about 2,500 trucks.
Close most crossings, inspect every truck at the rest, and Iran’s lifeline becomes a queue.
To that end, this month US Central Command established Task Force Iron Gate , charged with stopping weapons, sanctioned goods and illicit cash from crossing Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.
The goal is to make the overland route slow, expensive and payable only in the hard currency the regime no longer earns.
By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
And the plan is to have Iran’s neighbors, not American troops, enforce the blockade with their own border guards.
Three countries, Iraq, Pakistan and Turkmenistan, guard more than 60% of Iran’s land border.
But persuading them to take part in the effort has been tricky: Iraq has so far refused Washington’s request to close all but two of its crossings, and Pakistan has shuttered them intermittently.
CENTCOM needs to take action to strengthen the case for cooperation.
It must offer intelligence: The US must pledge to share data from American satellites, drones and financial investigators, so border commanders can know which trucks to open.
It must offer partnership: CENTCOM’s naval arm leads a coalition of more than 40 nations, including Iraq and Pakistan, that hunts smugglers at sea. Iron Gate should be that coalition on land.
And it must use its existing leverage: It’s hard to say no to the military force that has trained you for decades.
The US-led coalition trained and equipped Iraq’s border guards, Washington approved a $686 million upgrade of Pakistan’s F-16s last year, and CENTCOM paid for a border checkpoint on Turkmenistan’s frontier with Iran.
CENTCOM should make clear that future training, equipment and funding depend on cooperation at the Iranian border.
Treasury has sanctioned Iran’s rail and auto sectors, truck makers included.
It should back the task force by putting every freight forwarder, trucking company and inland port on notice that hauling the regime’s cargo means losing access to the dollar.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf predicted on Nov. 11 that the incoming Congress will pile political pressure on the White House.
Trump must prove him wrong. No deal has to mean no letup.
There’s no need for another major military campaign while economic pressure does the same work.
Save military force for the minelayers and missile crews that threaten ships and Americans.
Anything wider hands the regime the war it would use to hide a broken economy.
The sea is closed to the regime, and the sky is closing.
Close the roads, and it will be left alone with the 90 million Iranians it has robbed for 47 years.
Then it will have two choices: accept America’s terms, or answer to its own people.
Mark Dubowitz is chief executive of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, where Miad Maleki is a senior fellow.

Iran says 2 oil tankers hit mines near Strait of Hormuz, 1 sinks
Iran says 2 oil tankers hit mines near Strait of Hormuz, 1 sinks
Revolutionary Guard says sunken supertanker was carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil
Mustafa Melih Ahishali, Muhammet Torunlu and Rania Abushamala
ISTANBUL Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Sunday that two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, sinking one of the vessels.
The IRGC Navy said the tankers were attempting to use what it called an “unauthorized” route when the mine strikes triggered powerful explosions. It said one of the vessels, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, sank in the southern Gulf.
The force alleged that the tankers had switched off their navigation systems and tried to cross undetected with support from the US military.
The statement did not identify either vessel or give details on the crews.
Iran announced on July 12 that it had closed the strait again after the US resumed strikes on Iran. Tehran has warned it would target vessels that use routes other than those it designates or attempt to transit without its permission.
​​​​​​​The Strait of Hormuz is a major route for global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Disruptions to shipping through the waterway have heightened concerns over global energy supplies.

How Will the Market React to a Potential Fed Rate Hike in December? Here's What History Suggests.
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates at its Dec. 9 meeting. CME FedWatch data indicated an 86.8% probability of a 25-basis-point (one-quarter of a percentage point) hike to 4%–4.25% and a 13.2% probability of a 50-basis-point (half percentage point) hike to 4.25%–4.50% during trading on Nov. 11.
Investors have already started reacting to changing rate expectations. After October inflation exceeded expectations, the two-year Treasury yield jumped about 18 basis points on Nov. 10. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) fell 0.38% on that day. However, the large-cap stock index rebounded 1.3% on Nov. 11, helped by a rally in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Image source: Getty Images. History shows that stocks do not always fall after rate hikes. The market's response also depends on what investors expect from the Fed's future interest rate decisions.
On Dec. 16, 2015, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis points for the first time in nearly a decade. The S&P 500 gained 1.45% that day. Investors had anticipated the increase, and the Federal Reserve indicated that subsequent hikes would be gradual.
On Dec. 19, 2018, another 25-basis-points interest rate hike coincided with a 1.54% decline in the S&P 500. Investors were worried about slowing economic growth, while the Federal Reserve still projected additional interest rate increases. Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell also indicated that the central bank would continue reducing its bond holdings, a policy that withdraws liquidity from the financial system. This added to investors' concerns about tighter financial conditions.
However, the S&P 500 gained nearly 28% over the following 12 months, during which the Federal Reserve reversed course and cut interest rates three times in 2019.
The interest rate hike in March 2022 offers another example. The S&P 500 gained 2.24% on March 16, when the Federal Reserve began raising interest rates. However, the S&P 500 index lost 9.1% over the following 12 months, as inflation remained high and the central bank accelerated rate increases. The Russia-Ukraine war, slowing global growth, and recession fears also weighed on stocks.
These examples show why the market's immediate reaction to a rate hike does not necessarily indicate how stocks will perform over the following year.
A widely expected 25-basis-point hike in December may have a limited impact on stocks. However, a surprise 50-basis-point increase or signals of more rate hikes in 2027 could push Treasury yields higher and negatively impact stock prices.
In September 2026, Federal Reserve officials projected a median interest rate of approximately 4.1% at the end of both 2026 and 2027. The new projections in December 2026 could indicate whether policymakers now expect more increases. Higher interest rates can raise companies' borrowing costs and reduce what investors are willing to pay for their future earnings.
The pace of interest rate increases is also important. A Charles Schwab report examined 18 Federal Reserve tightening cycles since World War II. The S&P 500's average maximum 12-month decline following the first hike was 16% in faster-tightening cycles, compared with 12% in slower ones. These numbers measure the largest declines during those periods, not full-year returns.
The U.S. economy has remained resilient. Inflation-adjusted gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter. Employers also added 165,000 jobs in October 2026. Continued economic growth could help companies sustain sales and earnings despite higher interest rates.
However, not all businesses can manage tight financial conditions. The Federal Reserve's May 2026 Financial Stability Report found that many publicly traded companies remained well positioned to service their debt. However, some riskier borrowers with floating-rate loans faced greater debt-servicing pressures.
Stocks trading at premium valuations may face downward pressure if investors are not willing to pay a premium for future growth. Instead, companies with strong cash flow and reasonable valuations may be better positioned to withstand further rate increases.
Investors hoping to avoid potential losses from a December rate hike may consider selling stocks before the Federal Reserve's announcement and buying them again at lower prices. However, this strategy requires accurately predicting when stocks will decline and when they will recover. Morningstar found that between January 1990 and March 2026, the median gap between the S&P 500's 10 worst and 10 best trading days was just seven days.
Historical returns also suggest that rate hikes do not necessarily lead to prolonged stock market declines. LPL Research examined six Fed tightening cycles since 1994 and found that the S&P 500 gained an average 6.7% in the 12 months following the first hike. However, the absolute returns varied across the different time periods.
A widely expected December rate hike may affect stocks, but unexpected signals about future increases could trigger volatility. Long-term investors may be better served by maintaining diversified portfolios and focusing on companies' financial health rather than trying to predict the market's immediate reaction.

items.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
items.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
items.content:
Image caption, The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment
By Dearbail Jordan ,Â  Business reporter Â  and Â  Lily Jamali ,Â  North America Technology correspondent ,Â  Reporting from Palo Alto, CA
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
But while Alice Huang is said to have stepped down from her role as Megaspeed director near the end of 2023, there were suspicions that she was still heavily involved in the firm's operations, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS
C4ADS said that Huang was still "practically in control" of Megaspeed even after she had handed over the reins of the firm.
Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.
Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.
Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.
"That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme.
Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded.
The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated to lead Nvidia is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing.
The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside the company.
On Friday, Bessent had blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

items.title: 60 Minutes Transcript: Families of U.S. military members killed in Iran war want answers from the Pentagon - CBS News
items.summary: 60 Minutes Transcript: Families of U.S. military members killed in Iran war want answers from the Pentagon  CBS News
items.content:
There are many ways to measure the cost of the Iran war. The latest price tag from the Pentagon is $47 billion. But the war's heaviest toll has been levied on the more than 800 American service members wounded and the families of the 23 who have died.
Tonight on 60 Minutes, our monthslong investigation reveals the extent of the damage to U.S. positions in the Middle East. You'll also hear from Gold Star families. Their loved ones were killed in the first 24 hours of fighting when an Iranian drone struck an army command post in Kuwait. It was Iran's deadliest strike against the U.S. military and shattered any perception that American troops were beyond the reach of an enemy, skilled in a new type of warfare.
Joey Amor: There are soldiers that are signing up now that are going to go. And they have to trust that what happened to my wife isn't gonna happen to them.
Joey Amor's wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor was one of the first six Americans to die in the war . The fallen American service members were met at Dover Air Force Base by the president and top leaders.
Joey Amor: She was proud. She was constant. She was unwavering. She was dedicated.
Master Sgt. Amor served in the Army Reserve's 103rd Sustainment Command.
Joey Amor: I don't have anything nice to say about the 103rd.
Joey Amor: I love those soldiers. And my wife loved those soldiers. But the command of the 103rd has handled this so poorly. And if I'm bein' frank, it's-- it's on them. They killed my wife. They killed these soldiers. And it's not political. there are individuals in that command that made choices.
Those choices by command have been the focus of our eight-month-long investigation into the first American deaths of the war. The day after the attack, on March 2nd, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth insisted the troops there were well-protected .
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth: Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately we call it a squirter that makes its way through. And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified. But these are powerful weapons.
The U.S. military had built up a significant presence in the Middle East. But in the weeks leading up to the Iran war, the Pentagon moved 90% of its ground forces out of Kuwait and away from Iran, fearing retaliatory strikes. But some 70 members of the 103rd - which handles logistics - were sent closer to the threat, to this small army outpost - known as Port Shuaiba - about 65 miles from Iran.
Norah O'Donnell: How would you describe the installation at Port Shuaiba?
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: It was, some people have phrased it as a trailer park.
Major Stephen Ramsbottom was the 103rd's deputy chief of operations and a combat veteran.
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: The protection that was there was to stop car bombs and threats like that. There was nothing there designed to protect from an aerial attack.
Iran has developed an arsenal of kamikaze drones like these and Major Ramsbottom says the threat of a drone attack was well-known. It was raised to the unit commander, Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes. And Ramsbottom says he warned Maj. Gen. John Hinson - who oversaw logistics for the U.S. Central Command.
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: I brought it up in twice in various meetings-- basically saying, "Hey, I don't see how we're protected here."
Norah O'Donnell: And how did your leadership respond?
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: He said we don't have to worry about protection
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: Yes that's why I'm speaking up. I feel this is a, a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself, all the way down to my level. yes we just, we did not plan this well. And this needs to be a lesson that we learn.
Major Ramsbottom was not the only one concerned. We spoke with six soldiers who told us they had seen U.S. intelligence before the war started that put Port Shuaiba on an Iranian list of targets.
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: I saw those reports, there was definitely an X where we were.
In the week before the attack, soldiers asked for extra support.
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: That was command Sarn't Major that chimed in with, "Hey, we're gonna try to get this this counter drone system sent out to you."
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: No, it never arrived at Shuaiba. And we don't know if it was ever even ordered to or requested.
This past week, Major Ramsbottom filed this whistleblower complaint to Congress - demanding an investigation into why there was no "dedicated protection against one-way attack drones." He also claims "the site had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance."
Tanner Carson: We did not have the manpower nor the equipment for any kind of a mass casualty incident.
Tanner Carson was one of two civilian medics regularly stationed at the Port. He was surprised when, in late February, he heard dozens of soldiers from the 103rd were moving in.
Norah O'Donnell: What was your concern when you heard that you would have an increase in head count?
Tanner Carson: The lack of resources, the lack of additional manpower, the lack of additional transport capability, and the fact that we did not have any kind of a supply cache on site. Like, the only medical supplies that we had were what was in my truck.
Carson knew Master Sgt. Nicole Amor - he told us she had specifically asked him if there was a mass casualty plan.
Tanner Carson: She wanted to know, you know, "What's the plan if something were to happen?"
Norah O'Donnell: I mean, hearing that is kinda stunning. It's like she was concerned.
Tanner Carson: They all were. Anybody who came and asked those same questions, it was the same answer. "I have enough here to get you to the hospital and I have enough here to keep two of you alive at most."
The week before her death, Master Sgt. Amor told her husband that she was worried about her unit's safety.
Joey Amor: It's the only time in 15 years that I've ever heard her like that. She knew somethin' was comin'. They all knew somethin' was comin'.
The night the U.S. and Israel killed Iran's supreme leader in a joint strike, Iranian quadcopter drones can be seen in this video circling above Port Shuaiba. Soldiers told us five of these drones were spotted, likely conducting surveillance.
Men and women of the 103rd were running in and out of nearby bunkers.
Around 9 a.m. the next morning, the soldiers received the all-clear and went back to their workspace. Some 30 minutes later, the Iranian drone hit.
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: I remember just getting knocked to the ground. and it was like someone came up behind me and hit me in the back of the head with a baseball bat or something. Everything just went black.
Major Stephen Ramsbottom: It hit the center of the quadruple-wide trailer we were in
New video obtained by 60 Minutes shows black smoke billowing from the command post.
Norah O'Donnell: When you got to the scene, what did you see?
Tanner Carson: A mess. I could tell the building itself wasn't there anymore. And through the smoke you could see people laying on the ground, people carrying other bodies, people kinda limping together with one another.
Master Sgt. Amor was still breathing when soldiers loaded her into an SUV and drove her to a local Kuwaiti hospital.
Joey Amor: They were googling hospitals to try to take some of the soldiers to. That's absurd.
Norah O'Donnell: Do you think that if there had been a plan your wife would be alive today?
Among the American soldiers killed were Master Sgt. Noah Tietjens and Chief Warrant Officer Robert Marzan. We spoke with Tietjens' widow Michelle and Marzan's widow Tina.
Norah O'Donnell: You were one of the last to be notified. Why was that?
Tina Marzan: I think the drone hit them directly. And I don't know who knew that they were still in the building, in this metal shed that they were in. And I know they found his hat next to him.
Norah O'Donnell: They had to use DNA to identify him?
The attack on Port Shuaiba was one of many in the region
Our analysis of satellite imagery and new video shows the scale of destruction the Pentagon has never fully disclosed.
Since the start of the war, Iran has hit at least 31 U.S. military and diplomatic sites across eight countries, damaging hundreds of buildings and structures — from Saudi Arabia, to Kuwait, to Bahrain, where the headquarters of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet was destroyed.
Iran's strikes have continued for months, even after President Trump declared victory on April 1.
Three months later on July 17, Iranian missiles targeted housing units on a U.S. base in Jordan, killing three more American soldiers .
When American troops are killed in action, it falls on fellow soldiers to deliver the news – like the ones who visited Tina Marzan the night after her husband died at Port Shuaiba.
Tina Marzan: And immediately when you see them standing outside, you know. I just didn't want it to be real.
Tietjens prepared to share the news with their 13-year-old son.
Michelle Tietjens: I gathered a few items that my son would want. One of 'em was his dad's sweatshirt that he left at home, an Army little teddy bear, and I went back to my-- my-- where my son was, and I had to tell him Daddy wasn't comin' home.
Joey Amor tried to shield their 10-year-old daughter and 18-year-old son from the two soldiers walking up his driveway.
Joey Amor: And my daughter didn't understand. And my son said, "I know."
Norah O'Donnell: The worst thing in your life, and then also to share it with your children.
Joey Amor: What it's been like-- for us since then has been-- it's been a nightmare. when your baseline is you wake up and you roll over and your wife's not there, and that's your baseline and you know that she's never gonna be there again, and it's not because she's mad at you, it's because she doesn't exist anymore.
The Gold Star families told us they have received military honors and outreach from the Trump administration – but don't believe they've gotten the full story.
Norah O'Donnell: It has been eight months since the attack. What has the Pentagon told you?
Tina Marzan: The truth. Accountability. Just own it. Say, "Something went wrong and we didn't plan right." That's all that I want.
The Pentagon has declined to answer whether the 103rd was denied adequate force protection. The U.S. Army finished its investigation into the attack in June. This week the families are finally being briefed on the results.
Norah O'Donnell: If the Pentagon says the U.S. military did nothing wrong and that this is the cost of war, will you accept that?
Joey Amor: No. You trust your leadership to put you in the best possible position. And my wife's death, I already know, was preventable. I will not accept, "That's the cost of war."
We reached out to the two generals who allegedly ignored warnings about drone attacks, Maj. Gen. John Hinson and Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes. Neither responded. Yesterday, Army officials briefed Michelle Tietjens on the results of its Port Ahuaiba investigation – she told us they did not acknowledge any mistakes.

items.content:
Third time's the charm? Israel risks another Iran war without learning from past fail
Third time's the charm? Israel risks another Iran war without learning from past failures
Analysis: As Israel weighs a third war with Iran, Netanyahu and IDF chief Eyal Zamir face questions about the first two campaigns, their overstated achievements and whether another round of fighting can succeed without a clear strategic objective
The campaign for a third war with Iran in the space of a year and a half is in full swing. According to numerous reports on the subject, the two approaches dominating the debate share the same outlook but differ over timing and legitimacy.
One approach , led by the prime minister and the heads of security agencies suspected of personal loyalty to him, such as the Mossad chief and the national security adviser, is pushing for action now, preferably alongside the Americans but, if necessary, without them . The second approach, led by the IDF chief of staff and backed by the Jewish opposition and most of the media, holds that the situation is deeply troubling but not so urgent that a caretaker government should order an operation that would send millions of people rushing to shelters.
Once a new government is sworn in, and not necessarily long after it takes office, it would be an entirely different story, because the problem of "public trust" would supposedly have been resolved.
While the first approach reeks of political interests like a burning garbage dump, or at least of the knowledge that Netanyahu is capable of putting those interests ahead of everything else, the second is perceived as a more serious and responsible position because it combines professional analysis with consideration for the collective good.
In this context, the chief of staff personally enjoys considerable artillery cover, both from the usual ranks of military reporters and commentators who receive their information intravenously from the IDF Spokesperson's Unit, and from supporters of Gadi Eisenkot on television panels and opinion pages. That support stems from his role as a "gatekeeper" standing up to Netanyahu and his entourage, at least when it comes to Iran.
In Gaza, the party continues. If disagreements exist within the IDF's senior ranks, for example, they receive little meaningful attention. Who knows? Perhaps, by some miracle, as in the series "Pluribus," everyone has been infected with a virus that makes them think exactly like IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir.
Yet Zamir's approach to the issue cannot be allowed to pass without clear answers to some difficult questions. He was a full partner in presenting the two previous wars as resounding successes. Of the first, he said that Iran's nuclear program had been "set back by years." Of the second, he said, "We eliminated ... the weapons industries, the surface-to-air missile batteries and the surface-to-surface missile launchers." Even at the time, there were a few who emphasized the gaps between those grand declarations and the achievements on the ground, which were by no means insignificant. Entering another war requires the military, too, to explain those discrepancies.
After Operation Roaring Lion , Zamir seemed to ignore the third objective that Israel and the United States had fantasized about: toppling the ayatollahs' regime. It was as though this had been someone else's whim and he was merely the contractor responsible for carrying out the bombings. That ambiguity cannot continue, particularly after Netanyahu declared that this was the directive he had given the IDF. It was no coincidence that he chose to make that declaration at an officer graduation ceremony, right in front of the chief of staff.
If Zamir and others genuinely believe that another war is unavoidable, they must explain what will become of that directive, which Netanyahu says is the only way to fundamentally change the situation. For example, assuming that a regime in a country of 100 million people cannot be overthrown without American leadership, and even with the Americans it turned out, astonishingly, to be a little more complicated than some had imagined, is there still any point in entering the delightful reality of repeated rounds of fighting?
Trying to sell the public a third war with Iran without acknowledging the strategic failures of the previous two and the lies told about them is sheer folly, regardless of who is fronting the campaign: Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Zamir, Trump, military commentators eager for action or Yehuda Levi. We might as well tell the public that "third time's the charm." Given the past three years, there's a chance that might even work.

Felicity Bradstock is a writer and journalist based in Mexico City. She writes for energy websites and covers several other industries, as well as writing…
More than 50 major U.S. oil and gas companies earned over $130 billion in profits between April and September 2026.
Refiners and oil producers have benefited from elevated energy prices and disruptions to Middle Eastern supplies.
American consumers have faced billions in additional fuel costs as the war continues to disrupt global energy markets.
Several oil and gas companies in the United States have benefited from increased trade following the war in Iran that began in February, and from subsequent restrictions on international energy trade. Many countries have been forced to turn to alternative suppliers due to restrictions on movement through the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway connecting the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea, a shift that has allowed U.S. oil majors to help fill the gap.
The Strait of Hormuz has faced severe, ongoing restrictions and a functional blockade since late February 2026, following attacks on Iran by the United States and Israel, which led Tehran to respond by limiting movement through the waterway. Prior to the trade restrictions, the Strait of Hormuz was used to transport around one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).
In 2025, roughly 20 million barrels of oil and oil products passed through the waterway every day, equivalent to almost $600 billion in energy trade per year, according to estimates from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). As Iran continues to impose trade restrictions, several countries have been forced to halt energy exports , particularly in the Persian Gulf, resulting in a severe negative impact on certain economies.
Uncertainties about how and when the Strait of Hormuz may reopen, and what energy trade might look like going forward, have led many countries around the globe to rapidly seek new fuel suppliers. The recent trade restrictions have exposed vulnerabilities in global energy trade and demonstrated the importance of diversification – both in energy exports and in expanding production beyond fossil fuels to renewable alternatives.
A recent New York Times analysis suggests (conservatively) that U.S. oil firms have earned over $130 billion in profit this year, owing to higher fuel prices and increased demand for certain products. This assessment is based on the performance of over 50 major U.S. oil and gas companies, mainly producers and refiners, between April and September. By contrast, these companies earned less than $47 billion between them in the same period last year.
Some companies are seeing higher profits than others, particularly those in the U.S. refining industry. Several Middle Eastern and Russian refining facilities have been damaged in recent years due to ongoing conflicts, threatening the world’s refining capacity and allowing U.S. oil companies to step in to fill the gap.
U.S. companies can continue to operate safely and securely while several Middle Eastern refining companies must operate under dangerous conditions due to the ongoing conflict. In addition, U.S. oil and gas companies are largely sheltered from the high costs of shipping, as much of the oil they process is transported via pipeline.
Geoffrey Miller, a geopolitical analyst and editor of the Gulf States Insights newsletter, explained that the war in Iran “created a risk premium that U.S.-based operators are structurally well placed to monetise,” whereas Gulf producers were “hit hard by both higher costs and risks, along with physical damage, which makes their ability to benefit from the higher prices much more difficult.”
The largest U.S. oil and gas companies, Exxon Mobil and Chevron, have been two of the firms to profit most from the war, reporting sky-high third-quarter earnings in October. Exxon’s third-quarter profit more than doubled, while Chevron’s nearly tripled.
Nevertheless, the profits seen so far this year remain below those of 2022, directly following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent introduction of sanctions on various Russian energy products. In 2022, oil prices rose to an average of $100 a barrel, compared with around $90 a barrel between April and September this year.
As U.S. oil and gas companies continue to profit, consumers across the U.S. have been forced to pay more for energy and gasoline in recent months as constraints on international fuel supplies drive prices ever higher. Estimates suggest that U.S. consumers have spent an additional $147 billion – over $1,100 per household – on gasoline and diesel since the beginning of the war in Iran. The disparity has driven a political debate over who profits and who pays the price for the war.
The United States is not the only country to experience higher oil and gas profits in response to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with several European oil majors reporting higher-than-average earnings. Shell reported $12.06 billion in third-quarter earnings, roughly double what it earned in the same period last year. Meanwhile, France’s TotalEnergies more than doubled its third-quarter profit compared to 2025, at $8.26 billion.
As several oil and gas companies across the Middle East and Asia continue to see restrictions on energy production and trade due to ongoing conflict, damage to infrastructure, and restrictions on movement through the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. and European fossil fuel companies are expected to continue profiting from both the higher demand for fuel from these markets and elevated oil and gas prices.

Fed’s Collins: With risks on both sides, a steady and gradual pace of rate hikes is appropriate
By: Lallalit Srijandorn , FXStreet Tags: Federal Reserve
A steady sequence of modest interest rate hikes would help manage economic uncertainty more effectively, Boston Federal Reserve (Fed) President Susan Collins said on Saturday, explaining her support for that approach.
Inflation and employment figures suggest the Fed may need to raise rates further than recently anticipated.
Financial conditions could weigh on the economy more heavily than expected.
With risks on both sides, a steady, gradual approach to rate increases is appropriate.
There was a good case for leaving rates unchanged at the October FOMC meeting.
Bringing inflation back to 2% is critical for the Fed.
To address the high cost of living, the most effective step the Fed can take is to restore stable inflation.
The labour market is in a state of ‘unusual stability,’ and could strengthen further.
Longer-term inflation expectations are most likely to remain anchored.

How does the Federal Reserve’s role influence the US Dollar?
The Federal Reserve (Fed) sets US monetary policy with two objectives: maintaining price stability and promoting full employment. Adjustments to interest rates are its main means of pursuing these goals.
If prices climb too rapidly and inflation exceeds the Fed’s 2% target, the central bank increases interest rates. Higher borrowing costs across the economy make the US more attractive to international investors seeking a place for their funds, strengthening the US Dollar (USD).
Conversely, inflation below 2% or an excessively high Unemployment Rate may prompt the Fed to cut interest rates to stimulate borrowing. This puts pressure on the Greenback.
What is the schedule for the Fed’s monetary policy meetings?
At eight policy meetings each year, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) of the Federal Reserve (Fed) reviews the economy and decides on monetary policy.
Twelve Fed officials take part: the seven Board of Governors members, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and four of the other eleven regional Reserve Bank presidents. The latter serve rotating one-year terms.
How does Quantitative Easing (QE) work, and what does it mean for USD?
When conditions become extreme, the Federal Reserve may turn to Quantitative Easing (QE), a policy that substantially expands credit flows through a stalled financial system.
This unconventional measure is deployed during crises or periods of exceptionally low inflation. During the Great Financial Crisis in 2008, it was the Fed’s preferred tool. Under QE, the Fed prints additional Dollars to purchase high-grade bonds from financial institutions. The US Dollar typically weakens as a result.
How does Quantitative Tightening (QT) work, and why does it affect the US Dollar?
By reversing QE, quantitative tightening (QT) typically supports the US Dollar’s value. Under this policy, the Federal Reserve ceases bond purchases from financial institutions and, when bonds in its portfolio mature, does not reinvest the principal in new bonds.

Saudi, Iraqi Oil Replace Iranian Crude in China: Report
Saudi and Iraqi oil has begun replacing Iranian crude in China as Tehran's exports to the world's largest oil importer have plunged under the impact of a US blockade on its ports along the Arabian Gulf, imposed in July, Bloomberg’s Asharq Business website reported on November 15, citing vessel-tracking firm Vortexa.
Iranian oil exports to China fell to less than 100,000 barrels per day in October, down from around 1.4 million barrels per day before the war broke out in late February, Vortexa’s data showed.
The shift is creating an opportunity for major Gulf producers to expand their market shares in China, as the report said that Iranian inventories of crude loaded onto oil tankers and vessels used for floating storage, which Tehran had accumulated in the months before the war and the blockade, are now close to being depleted.
This is reducing its ability to continue meeting Chinese demand from available stockpiles, Vortexa argued.
Chinese buyers of Iranian crude have turned to Russian oil and other non-sanctioned grades, including Venezuelan crude, to make up for the loss of Iranian supplies, the firm added.
However, the firm said, these alternatives have not fully offset Iranian volumes, opening the door for Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and other Gulf producers to capture additional market share in China.

Uncertainty Abounds in a U.S.-Iran “No War-No Peace” Environment - The Soufan Center
Intelbrief / Uncertainty Abounds in a U.S.-Iran “No War-No Peace” Environment
Uncertainty Abounds in a U.S.-Iran “No War-No Peace” Environment
Perceiving that they each have the strategic upper hand, U.S. and Iranian leaders appear unable to reach a settlement, even as the substantive gaps between their positions have narrowed.
Trump has decided not to implement threats to escalate military action or pursue a diplomatic settlement, opting instead to rely on severe economic pressure to compel Iranian leaders to capitulate.
President Trump’s repeated messaging that the U.S. goal is to change Iran’s regime increases the potential for pre-emptive Iranian escalation.
Regional leaders continue to try to mediate a resolution and plan for a “no war-no peace” scenario, at least until Trump’s term ends in early 2029.
U.S., Iranian, and other regional leaders see no clear pathway to break out of the strategic stalemate prevailing in the Gulf more than eight months after the U.S. and Iran launched Operation Epic Fury . President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intended the operation to oust the regime that has ruled Iran since 1979, perceiving regime leaders as weakened by major domestic unrest in January. After subsequent cycles of attack and retaliation, the U.S. and Iran each believe it holds a strategic upper hand. Tehran and Washington appear reluctant to take the remaining steps to achieve a war-ending settlement, perceiving that any expression of flexibility signals weakness. Leaders on both sides accept that escalation is unlikely to shift the strategic balance in either direction, or alter their adversary’s terms for a settlement. The stalemate has left regional leaders with no choice but to plan for a “no war-no peace” scenario that could last for years.
Trump and his team provided the region with some relief last week by signaling that, barring a provocation by Iran or its ally, the Houthi movement in Yemen , he will not implement threats to escalate military action against Iranian (or Houthi) targets. After a meeting at the White House last Monday with Qatar’s Prime Minister, Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Trump said U.S. military operations against Iran were “effectively over.” In other interviews, Trump indicated that he was responding to pressure from regional leaders, who are fearful of Iranian retaliation, not to escalate. Still, with a war-ending accord elusive and U.S. officials continuing to build military capacity off Iran’s coast, regional leaders are girding for the damage Iran will inflict on their infrastructure should major combat flare anew.  In a speech last week, Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), said the region should “prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted.”
As they analyze a range of possible scenarios, regional leaders have expressed frustration that a decisive end to the war eludes them. Compounding their anxiety, Trump last week signaled he is not eager for a settlement. In statements and speeches, Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicated the U.S. will rely on its economic pressure campaign, centered on a naval blockade , to instill additional flexibility in Iranian negotiating positions before pursuing a deal in earnest. In a post on his Truth Social account, Trump announced he was ending Vice President J.D. Vance’s renewed outreach to Iranian leaders in search of an accord. Vance had represented the U.S. in the talks that led to the failed June Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). The Vice President also took the initiative in recent weeks to directly engage, in writing, IRGC Major General Mohsen Reza’i, the hardliner at the helm of Iran’s main decision-making body, the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). The Trump post stated: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” His post continued: “I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention” on a task force created to curb fraud in U.S. social welfare programs. The Trump shift away from diplomacy not only disappointed the region, but risks provoking Iran to take pre-emptive military action that it has threatened.
Trump’s reference to the U.S. Navy’s success in helping protect commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz reflects his belief that U.S. strategy is benefiting strategically from the diplomatic stalemate. Global energy experts assess that the current flow of oil exports out of the Strait is nearly 80 percent of pre-war levels — a figure that accounts for the U.S. naval blockade, which is preventing Iran from moving any oil out of the Gulf. But Iran remains a threat to the global economy. At least 10 ships were hit by Iran in the first 10 days of November, after 37 attacks in October, which was the highest ?monthly tally since the conflict began in late February.
Senior officials of Qatar and Pakistan, the leading regional mediators, express regret that Trump is pulling back from diplomacy just as negotiators were making substantial progress. Officials close to the mediation efforts note the Iranian and U.S. core demands are no longer substantively far apart. Trump and his team have acknowledged an accord will require the U.S. to provide significant economic sanctions relief, including the release of blocked Iranian assets. Iranian leaders tell journalists they accept that any agreement will require verifiable steps to ensure Iran’s nuclear program could only be used for peaceful purposes, including allowing the dilution of a stockpile of 60 percent enriched uranium. In the latest U.S.-Iran exchanges, as reported by some regional media outlets, Iranian negotiators expressed willingness to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz as part of a settlement, apparently relaxing Iran’s insistence on “managing’ commercial traffic using routes along Iran’s Persian Gulf coast. Iranian leaders have denied altering any of their core positions, complicating assessments of whether the two sides are close to an agreement.
Further clouding the prospects for a settlement, Trump and his team continue to send mixed messages about their intended goals. Since the early days of the war, Trump has repeatedly stressed that the goal of the U.S. war effort is to permanently end any possibility for Iran to develop a nuclear weapon. In the latest exchanges, U.S. officials are demanding that a settlement not defer a nuclear accord for further discussion — a postponement that U.S. officials consider a key flaw of the June MOU . However, in recent interviews, Trump has sometimes returned to the original objective of the war — ending the Tehran regime’s control over Iran.  In an interview with commentator Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump asserted that, if the regime remained in power by the end of his term in early 2029: “Yes, that would be a [U.S.] defeat. I would say that would be a defeat. Absolutely.” The repeated U.S. citation of a regime change goal reinforces the Iranian perception that the conflict is existential, and deprives Iran of a viable off-ramp — increasing the potential for Iranian pre-emptive escalation.
Unsure when, or even if, the U.S.-Iran conflict might conclude, leaders of the region are scrambling to assemble a new security architecture to defend against an Iranian regime still in power, hardened, and bent on ousting U.S. forces from the region. The region’s base case holds that a “no war-no peace” environment might prevail until the end of President Trump’s term in January 2029, and possibly beyond. The no war-no peace scenario not only keeps the region on a hair-trigger for further combat but also leaves the Arab Gulf states bereft of new investment and unable to advance their ambitious economic diversification programs.
No matter how the U.S.-Iran conflict evolves or ends, the security architecture of the Gulf region will change. The future U.S. security mission in the Gulf, according to experts, will be bounded – forgoing regime change efforts and focused on containing Iranian power, preventing it from acquiring a nuclear weapon, and protecting the Arab Gulf states from Iranian intimidation. Within those limits, the U.S. will remain the main Gulf security guarantor , as no Gulf leader has identified a combination of alternative security partners capable of replacing Washington. In light of their vulnerability to Iranian drones and short-range missiles, the U.S.-manned bases in the Gulf are not likely to be rebuilt to the scale reached before the conflict. And it is a near certainty that far fewer than the 40,000 U.S. forces forward-positioned will be deployed there. Some postulate the U.S. will move back to the “over the horizon” presence that existed prior to the 1991 war against Saddam Hussein’s regime, or to a more flexible, contingency-driven base access model. Under that latter structure, the U.S. would be able to surge forces into the Gulf in the event of a crisis and move forces around as necessary. Experts recommend that regional leaders begin constructing the future security architecture before their options narrow.

In calling for an end to the Iran War, Vance walks a fine line with Trump A rift is opening up between President Trump and Vice President Vance when it comes to the Iran War. NPR's Ayesha Rascoe talks to Susan Glasser, staff writer at the New Yorker.
In calling for an end to the Iran War, Vance walks a fine line with Trump
In calling for an end to the Iran War, Vance walks a fine line with Trump

A rift is opening up between President Trump and Vice President Vance when it comes to the Iran War. NPR's Ayesha Rascoe talks to Susan Glasser, staff writer at the New Yorker.
AYESHA RASCOE, HOST: The day after Republicans suffered a major defeat in the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance posted a list of what Republicans could do to win back disillusioned voters. No. 1 - end the war in Iran. President Trump said he didn't disagree. But last week he posted, quote, "we don't need a deal with Iran." Instead of focusing on Iran, Trump said he was asking Vance to turn his complete and total attention to corruption and crime in cities and states run by Democrats. Joining us now is Susan Glasser, staff writer at The New Yorker. Thank you so much for joining us. SUSAN GLASSER: Oh, great to be with you. RASCOE: Did you read President Trump's post as a response to Vance's criticism of the war? GLASSER: I mean, not to be too blunt, but basically, you have the president of the United States saying to his own vice president, yeah. You're kind of fired from the most important issue that we have, which is how to resolve this unresolved and unwon conflict in the Middle East. If anything, because of how overwhelming the scale of the Democratic victory was in the elections, we've kind of understated the extent to which it is a remarkable thing to have had Vice President Vance publicly blame the president's top foreign policy priority for that overwhelming defeat. Of course, we know Donald Trump. He's furious about this. RASCOE: When Vance said the war is the problem, one thing that stood out to me is he kind of was talking about it as if he wasn't in the administration. Like, he didn't put himself in it. GLASSER: No. I think the big-picture context here, Ayesha, is clearly that Vice President Vance feels his chances, such as they are, for becoming president after Trump slipping away, largely due to the war. Donald Trump, of course, campaigned in 2024 saying he was the candidate of no new wars. And Vance was specifically selected from what you might call the real MAGA America First wing of the Republican Party. For him, this is even more foundational. His people have gone to great lengths, it seems to me, to put out in news reports that he was against the war from the beginning in the private councils that the president had, even though it has technically been his portfolio since the spring to negotiate an end to the conflict with Iran. Obviously, that has not succeeded. There are very dim prospects for any kind of success in a negotiated peace anytime very soon. I think for Vance, it just underscores the problem that American vice presidents have in general, which is to say it is very, very difficult as an incumbent vice president to win election as president. Only two presidents - George H. W. Bush managed to do this in 1988, after two terms of Ronald Reagan. You have to go all the way back to the 19th century before there's another incumbent vice president who managed the feat. RASCOE: Do you look at this as a breakup between Vance and Trump, maybe emotionally if not publicly? (LAUGHTER) GLASSER: It certainly wouldn't be unprecedented with this particular president, who not only fell out with his first vice president. But, you know, it all ended so badly that they're chanting, hang Mike Pence, because he won't do what Donald Trump wanted him to do on January 6. So the odds, it seems to me, based on Trump's history, were always quite high for JD Vance to have a very difficult time. RASCOE: Would it not be, I guess, the biggest irony if it were to happen that Trump leaves office, and it is up to the next president to deal with this war in the Middle East? Is that not a great irony for the president who was supposed to start no new wars? GLASSER: Absolutely. Not only is it a great irony. I - it's a very real possibility that the Iranians may continue in this nether state over the next couple years. Often, wars and conflicts do end not by the leaders who start them. Because they have so much invested politically and in terms of their own legacy in the conflict, it's harder for them to end wars. So historically, that is an analogy. And I'm mindful of the fact that Donald Trump - you know, he sort of came of age in the 1980s. And that image of Jimmy Carter, for him, was basically the definition of American weakness. And as you know, Donald Trump has almost a - sort of a cult of the idea of strength. So it would be a bitter pill, indeed, for him to swallow if the Iranians did to him some version of what they did to Jimmy Carter, which is to slowly strangle Carter's presidency. RASCOE: That's Susan Glasser. She's a staff writer at The New Yorker. Thank you so much for joining us. GLASSER: Great to be with you.

Donald Trump has pursued “the most idiosyncratic and unsuccessful” US foreign policy in living memory, said Max Boot in The Washington Post .
“Even among Republicans, there is little support for annexing Greenland , seizing Venezuela’s oil , waging a cold war with Canada , cutting off Ukraine, insulting and indiscriminately tariffing allies, buying diesel from Russia ” and “launching a war on Iran”. But most senior Republicans have been “too cowed” to protest, until now.
After last week’s “shellacking” in the midterms , Vice President J.D. Vance baldly stated on X that “the reason we lost is the war”. Trump himself had to admit that this is “largely true”; and this week, he said the war was “effectively over”, that negotiations to end it were under way, and that more attacks on Iran were “highly unlikely”.

Well, maybe, said Arta Moeini and Brett Erickson on UnHerd . But the president has been known to change his mind, and the danger of renewed conflict remains high. Trump is under “immense pressure to prove he is still in control”, and whatever constraints he now faces domestically, he retains considerable freedom to conduct foreign policy. A third aircraft carrier strike group is on course to reach the Middle East by the end of this month, building up the strength of US forces in the region to the level they were at at the start of the war.
Trump could attack Iran again, said Barak Ravid on Axios . But it would be “highly unpopular” – because it would drive oil prices up – and would probably not yield “a better military result”. The alternative is the peace negotiations. The difficulty is that Trump is making big demands: the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the end of Iran’s nuclear programme . The Iranians are in no mood to make concessions. Tehran, according to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is asking not just for an end to the naval blockade and sanctions, but for billions in frozen assets, and reparations from the US.
There is a third option, said William Hague in The Times – for the US to carry on strangling Iran’s economy. With the last of the oil revenues from shipments sent out before the US blockade petering out, and inflation soaring, this is likely to be the most effective way of forcing Tehran to seek terms.
Trump will have to be patient, which does not come easily to him. He’ll also need to show that he can be trusted to honour any agreement; and he’ll probably have to accept some limited, independently verified Iranian nuclear activity. “Yes, that would look remarkably like the 2015 agreement that Trump hated so much.” But it is likely to be “the only path” out of the trap he has created for himself .
